questions.q: Why does a 30-40 slide technical deck typically fail as a board-level security report?
options: Boards are not legally permitted to view more than 5 slides at a time
PDF decks cannot be presented in a boardroom setting
Technical decks are always factually inaccurate
It is built from the security team's point of view — everything that was done — rather than from the board's point of view of whether risk is controlled and what needs a decision
questions.explain: A board has limited meeting time for security and needs a report built around its own decision-making role, not a comprehensive account of everything the security team did.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the six elements a working board-level security report contains, according to this lesson?
options: A full list of every firewall rule currently deployed
The personal performance reviews of each security engineer
A headline risk posture statement — improving, stable, or worsening, and why
The complete source code of any internally built security tooling
questions.explain: The headline risk posture is the single most important line in the report, stating in one or two sentences whether risk is improving, stable, or worsening and why.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a board report needs "a clear ask" as one of its elements?
options: Because without an ask, the report is a status update rather than a governance input, and boards notice the difference
Because every board meeting legally requires a budget request regardless of content
Because the ask is only a formality with no real effect on the meeting
Because it replaces the need for any trended metrics
questions.explain: A clear ask — approving budget, accepting a risk, approving a policy change, or confirming no action is needed — is what makes the report a governance input rather than purely informational.

questions.q: What does the NACD Director's Handbook on Cyber-Risk Oversight, cited in this lesson, tell directors to expect from cyber risk reporting?
options: That cyber risk should never be discussed at the board level under any circumstances
That only the CISO's direct reports are allowed to attend the meeting where it's presented
That it should be reported the same way other enterprise risks are — in business terms, with quantified exposure where possible, tied to decisions the board actually owns
That cyber risk reporting should rely exclusively on raw vulnerability scan output
questions.explain: The NACD Handbook, produced with the Internet Security Alliance, explicitly warns against handing boards purely technical detail and instead calls for business-framed, decision-relevant reporting.

questions.q: What is the typical reporting cadence described in this lesson for board-level security reports, and what is explicitly NOT bound to that same cadence?
options: Monthly reporting to the full board, with every item including incidents bound to that same monthly cycle
Quarterly reporting to the relevant board committee, with escalation of a significant security incident handled outside that fixed cycle
Annual reporting only, with no provision for incidents at all
Weekly reporting directly to shareholders, with incidents folded into the same weekly update
questions.explain: Most organizations report on a quarterly cadence to a relevant committee, but a significant incident is escalated as it happens rather than waiting for the next scheduled meeting — the subject of the next lesson.
